Watts to Amps at 120V — US Standard Circuit Guide

Single-phase AC path

Current, voltage, and power factor feeding a real watt result

AC pages need power factor context, so the visual connects outlet voltage, current draw, PF, and breaker planning.

Formula Amps = Watts / (120V x PF)

Quick answer

Use this calculator to convert AC current into real watts with voltage and power factor.

Single-phase AC loads can be resistive or inductive. Resistive loads may be near PF 1.00, while motors, compressors, and HVAC equipment often need a lower power factor.

Amps = Watts / (120V x PF)

Inputs to check before calculating

  • Use the correct nominal voltage for the circuit.
  • Enter measured current or nameplate running current.
  • Use realistic PF for motors, compressors, and transformer loads.
  • Compare the result with breaker and continuous-load limits.

Example: 1,200 watts at 120 volts

At 120 volts, a 1,200 watt load draws 10 amps before AC power-factor adjustments. Use the power factor field when the equipment is a motor, compressor, inverter, or other inductive load.

Best use cases

  • US outlets
  • Appliance current
  • Breaker planning
  • single-phase AC load planning with clear unit labels.

Common mistake to avoid

Do not use DC-style amps x volts for every AC load when the equipment has a lower power factor.

How to use the result

Use the watt result for appliance planning, branch-circuit checks, and comparison with the main amps to watts formula.

Accuracy and safety note

Calculator output is a planning estimate. Final breaker sizing, wire gauge, derating, voltage-drop limits, equipment protection, and code compliance should be verified with manufacturer documentation and a qualified electrician or engineer.

For the broad formula, reference table, and breaker planning context, start with the main Amps to Watts Calculator.

FAQ

Watts to Amps at 120V — US Standar FAQ

Fast answers before you use the calculator or compare formulas.

15A How many watts is 15 amps at 120V?

15 amps at 120V equals 1,800 watts (15 × 120 = 1,800). This is the maximum capacity of a standard 15A household circuit. For continuous loads, the NEC 80% rule limits you to 1,440 watts on this circuit.

20A How many watts is 20 amps at 120V?

20 amps at 120V equals 2,400 watts. Kitchen and bathroom outlets are typically on 20A circuits. The continuous load limit is 1,920 watts (80% of 2,400).

MAX What is the maximum wattage for a 120V outlet?

A standard 120V, 15A outlet can handle 1,800 watts maximum (15 × 120). A 120V, 20A outlet handles 2,400 watts. However, for devices running more than 3 hours continuously, stay below the 80% threshold: 1,440W on a 15A circuit, 1,920W on a 20A circuit.

240 Why do some appliances need 240V instead of 120V?

High-power appliances like dryers (5,500W), EV chargers (7,680W), and central AC (3,600W) need more watts than a 120V circuit can safely deliver. At 120V, a 5,500W dryer would draw 46 amps — far exceeding standard circuit limits. At 240V, it draws only 23 amps, which fits a 30A circuit safely.

PF Do I need power factor for 120V household calculations?

For most household loads (lights, heaters, toasters, hair dryers), power factor is 1.00 or very close, so the simple formula Watts = Amps × 120 is sufficient. Use power factor only for motor-driven appliances like refrigerators (PF 0.80–0.90), window AC units (PF 0.85), and large workshop tools.

OUT How many 120V outlets can I put on one circuit?

The NEC does not set a fixed number of outlets per circuit, but the total load must stay within the breaker rating. A 15A/120V circuit handles 1,800W max. Add up the wattage of everything plugged in. In practice, 8–10 general-purpose outlets on a 15A circuit is common when not all are loaded simultaneously.
